issues.legal_issue: Courts cannot adjudicate disputes concerning the accession of a former Indian State and its acceptance by the Dominion of India.
material_facts: The former rulers acceded to the Dominion of India, and the Dominion accepted the accessions.
The dispute arose from the accessions and their acceptance.
issues.conclusion: The accessions and their acceptance were acts of State beyond municipal court review; after the Constitution, Article 363 and the proviso to Article 131 barred courts from settling disputes arising from them. Courts could register the fact of accession.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 363 and the proviso to Article 131 of the Constitution, and referred to section 6 of the Government of India Act, 1935, concerning accession. It held that accessions and their acceptance were acts of State that municipal courts could not review.

predicates.accession_dispute_proceeding: A proceeding asks a court to settle a dispute arising from a former state's accession or its acceptance.
predicates.accession_accepted_by_dominion: The Dominion accepted the former state's accession.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns an accession accepted by the Dominion, courts cannot adjudicate the accession dispute.

issues.legal_issue: A government cannot invoke an act of State to justify action against a person who is its own citizen.
material_facts: The challenged revocation was an act of the State after the Constitution came into force.
The petitioners and the government officials seeking to enforce the revocation were citizens of India.
The lands were within the territory of India.
issues.conclusion: A State Government has no right to do anything in the nature of an act of State, and an act of State cannot be exercised against the government's own citizens.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the Constitution's establishment of a common citizenship and sovereign democratic order, including Article 5. It applied the principle that there can be no act of State between a sovereign and its own subject, referring to Johnstone v. Pedlar and Walker v. Baird; it also discussed Mayor of Lyons v. East India Company.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_state_action and post_constitution_state_action and state_invokes_act_of_state and affected_person_is_citizen

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_action: A person brings a constitutional challenge to action taken by a government.
predicates.post_constitution_state_action: The government takes the challenged action after the constitutional order has come into force.
predicates.state_invokes_act_of_state: The government claims its action is an act of State.
predicates.affected_person_is_citizen: The person affected by the action is a citizen of the state taking it.

issues.definition: When a government invokes an act of State to defend post-constitutional action challenged by one of its citizens, it cannot rely on that defence.

issues.legal_issue: Post-constitutional revocation of an unresumed property grant could not be defended as an act of State and violated the grantees' fundamental rights.
material_facts: The former rulers made absolute grants of the villages to the petitioners before the Constitution came into force.
The grants had not been resumed by the former rulers or confiscated by the Dominion before the Constitution came into force.
The petitioners had rights to remain in possession when the Constitution came into force.
After the Constitution came into force, the State Government revoked the grants and sought to enforce the revocation.
The State did not claim that the revocation could be saved under another provision of law if it could not be defended as an act of State.
issues.conclusion: The revocation violated Article 31(1) and Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The petitioners were entitled to a writ under Article 32(2) restraining enforcement of the revocation and directing restoration of possession if it had been taken.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the Constitution eliminated arbitrary and despotic power over citizens and property. It applied Article 31(1), Article 19(1)(f), and Article 32(2). In considering whether property rights survived a change of sovereignty, it discussed Mayor of Lyons v. East India Company, Forester v. Secretary of State for India in Council, and other authorities on recognition or waiver of existing rights; it did not decide whether the grants could have been set aside through ordinary proceedings or legislation.

rule.if: constitutional_property_challenge and pre_constitution_grant_in_effect and grant_not_resumed_before_constitution and post_constitution_executive_revocation and no_other_legal_basis_claimed

predicates.constitutional_property_challenge: A grantee challenges government action affecting a property interest through a constitutional proceeding.
predicates.pre_constitution_grant_in_effect: A grant of property made before the constitutional order came into force remained in effect when that order began.
predicates.grant_not_resumed_before_constitution: The former ruler or the Dominion had not resumed or confiscated the granted property before the constitutional order began.
predicates.post_constitution_executive_revocation: The government later revoked the grant through executive action.
predicates.no_other_legal_basis_claimed: The government did not claim that the revocation was authorized on another legal basis if it could not be defended as an act of State.

issues.definition: When an unresumed pre-constitutional property grant is revoked by post-constitutional executive action challenged on constitutional grounds, and no other legal basis is claimed, the revocation violates fundamental property rights and warrants writ relief.
